title: LINQ to Objects versus remote query providers (in-memory vs server)
hook: LINQ to Objects runs every operator in your process against data already in memory. A remote provider like SQL translates only a subset of C# — mixing them without a clear boundary is how import code works on a list but times out on a table.

blocks.text: LINQ to Objects is System.Linq.Enumerable's implementation over any IEnumerable<T> already in the process: arrays, List<T>, Dictionary values, File.ReadLines results, or parsed CSV rows. Lambdas can call any C# you could call in a foreach — pattern matching, extension methods, StringComparison, switch expressions. Deferred execution still applies. This is the right default for import pipelines, in-memory reporting after you already loaded data, and deserialized JSON payloads.

entries.plainDefinition: Enumerable's in-process LINQ implementation. Full C# in lambdas; runs on data already in memory.
An IQueryProvider that translates expression trees to a server language like SQL.
entries.example: Entity Framework Core translating Where to a SQL WHERE clause.

entries.plainDefinition: A filter the provider can rewrite to its remote language — usually property access, constants, and basic string methods.
ToList or AsEnumerable that pulls remote data into memory before running rich C#.
entries.example: var rows = remoteQuery.ToList(); // then filter with full C#

blocks.text: CSV import, Redis JSON deserialization, and already-loaded attempt lists belong in LINQ to Objects. A remote provider is a different contract with a smaller language — not a faster List. Copy-pasting an in-memory query onto IQueryable and shipping it is the most common migration failure. The interview-level move: keep translatable predicates boring, then pull to objects with ToList before using the rest of C#.

blocks.title: When to materialize
blocks.body: If you need StringComparison, custom methods, pattern matching, or C# 14 extension properties in a filter, do it after ToList on an in-memory sequence — or after the remote chain's ToList wall.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Data already in memory?
items.body: Use LINQ to Objects on IEnumerable. Full C# available in every lambda.

items.title: Data on a remote server?
items.body: Use IQueryable with a provider. Keep predicates translatable.

items.title: Need rich C# on remote data?
items.body: Pull with ToList first (the wall), then run LINQ to Objects on the result.

items.title: Measure, don't assume
items.body: LINQ to Objects is not slower than foreach by law. Allocations from delegates and iterators are the real cost.

snippet.label: CSV import with LINQ to Objects
snippet.code:
public static IReadOnlyList<AttemptRow> ParseAttempts(IEnumerable<string> lines) =>
    lines
        .Skip(1)                                          // skip header row
        .Select(line => line.Split(','))                  // split columns
        .Where(cols => cols.Length >= 3 && cols[0] is not "")
        .Select(cols => new AttemptRow(cols[0], cols[1], int.Parse(cols[2])))
        .ToList();                                        // materialize before stream closes

public sealed record AttemptRow(string AttemptId, string Status, int Score);
snippet.explanation: Skip/Select/Where run in process. ToList materializes before the file enumerator is lost. Pattern cols[0] is not "" is ordinary C# in a Func.

snippet.label: Keep the wall explicit after import
snippet.explanation: OrdinalIgnoreCase is trivial in memory and historically awkward for some SQL providers. Doing it after ParseAttempts.ToList is honest and predictable.

snippet.label: What a remote provider may reject
snippet.explanation: Remote providers accept a subset of C#. DateTime.Now, string.Format, and switch expressions are common translation failures. Materialize, then use rich C#.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Copy-pasting an in-memory query onto IQueryable and shipping it. Leaving a query over File.ReadLines un-materialized after the stream closes. Micro-optimizing LINQ versus foreach before measuring allocations on the submit path. Assuming a remote provider is just a faster List.

blocks.text: LINQ to Objects is Enumerable over materialized or streaming in-memory sequences — full C# in Func lambdas, deferred iterator allocations on every operator. CSV import, Redis JSON, and parsed attempt lists belong here: **ToList()** before the file stream closes is the materialization wall. Remote IQueryable is a different contract with a translatable subset — copy-pasting in-memory LINQ fails at runtime. On hot in-memory paths, measure **iterator allocations** (WhereIterator, SelectIterator, delegate captures) with dotMemory; use **TryGetNonEnumeratedCount** when you need Count without walking a List twice. **Parallel LINQ (PLINQ)** via AsParallel() partitions in-memory snapshots for CPU-bound aggregation — pointer only when profiling shows single-threaded LINQ is the bottleneck; it does not apply to IQueryable providers. How to prove it in production: BenchmarkDotNet foreach versus LINQ on the submit path; allocation diff before/after folding three Where into one.

snippet.label: PLINQ pointer — measured opt-in only
snippet.explanation: Senior answer mentions PLINQ as a follow-up for CPU-bound in-memory aggregation after snapshot — not as the first fix for deferred execution bugs.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Copy-pasting LINQ to Objects onto IQueryable without checking translation — runtime NotSupportedException. Leaving File.ReadLines query un-materialized — empty results after dispose. Saying LINQ is always slower than foreach without measuring iterator allocations. Leading with PLINQ for every performance question. Strong answer: right flavor, ToList wall, measure allocations, PLINQ as measured CPU-bound opt-in.

interviewTakeaways: LINQ to Objects = Enumerable + in-memory sequences + full C# Func lambdas + deferred iterator allocations.
CSV, Redis JSON, and loaded attempt lists belong here; ToList before stream closes.
TryGetNonEnumeratedCount avoids double walk for Count on ICollection-backed sources.

60s: LINQ to Objects is in-process Func LINQ with iterator allocations. Materialize with ToList at boundaries. Remote IQueryable is a different translatable contract. PLINQ AsParallel is measured CPU-bound opt-in on snapshots, not default.
Follow-up: when would you replace LINQ with a for-loop on a hot path?
commonPitfalls: Copy-pasting an in-memory query onto IQueryable — fails translation at run time; rejected in senior loops.
Strong answer: keep translatable predicates on provider; ToList wall; then LINQ to Objects with full C#.
Leaving a query over File.ReadLines un-materialized after the stream closes — enumeration yields nothing.
Micro-optimizing LINQ versus foreach before measuring iterator allocations on the submit path.
